props.title: Winged Migration

sections.content: Winged Migration revolutionized nature documentary filmmaking through its breathtaking aerial cinematography following migrating birds across all seven continents. Director Jacques Perrin spent four years with teams of pilots and cinematographers using ultralight aircraft, gliders, and hot air balloons to capture unprecedented intimate footage of birds in flight. This groundbreaking approach influenced later works like March of the Penguins (2005) and Earth (2007), establishing a new standard for immersive nature documentaries that prioritize visual poetry over traditional narration.

sections.content: The technical innovations of Winged Migration sparked a renaissance in wildlife cinematography. Films like Chasing Coral (2017) and My Octopus Teacher (2020) built on its legacy of patience and proximity to capture unprecedented animal behavior. Perrin's team raised many of the birds from birth to acclimate them to the filming equipment, a controversial but effective technique that allowed for the closest bird-in-flight footage ever recorded at that time. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Nature Documentaries

The film's success paved the way for more artistically ambitious nature documentaries. Planet Earth (2006) and its sequel Planet Earth II (2016) adopted similar techniques of prolonged observation and intimate cinematography. The BBC's One Life (2011) directly referenced Winged Migration's approach to creating narrative arcs around animal subjects without anthropomorphizing them. This balance between scientific observation and artistic presentation has become the gold standard for contemporary wildlife filmmaking.
